Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Federal regulators announced $7.1 million in fines against American Airlines on Thursday over maintenance issues and problems with its drug- and alcohol-testing programs. American Airlines was fined for allowing aircrafts to fly while they knew they needed repairs. "The FAA believes the large total amount of the fine for these violations is appropriate because American Airlines was aware that appropriate repairs were needed, and instead deferred maintenance," the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement announcing the decision. "In intentionally continuing to fly the aircraft, the carrier did not follow important safety regulations intended to protect passengers and crew." American can still appeal the fines, the FAA said. The FAA also found the airline maintained inadequate drug- and alcohol-testing programs and failed to inspect safety lighting on a "timely" basis. The Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier said Thursday evening that it disagreed with the findings and called the penalties "excessive." "In accordance with FAA procedures for handling these matters, we have requested to meet with the FAA after we have had time to thoroughly review their findings, so that we may discuss the issues," the airline said in a written statement. "Since these matters are ongoing with the FAA, we will not have any further comment at this time." Nearly $4.5 million of the proposed fines stem from American's continued operation of two MD-83 jetliners in December 2007 after pilots reported problems with the autopilot systems, the FAA said. The two planes were flown a combined 58 times before the problems were corrected -- and one flew 10 times after an FAA inspector notified the airline that it had wrongly deferred needed repairs. In one incident, the autopilot disconnected during a landing on December 21, the FAA said. "American technicians did not check for the actual problem, and instead deferred maintenance using an inappropriate MEL (minimum equipment list) item. The plane flew another 36 passenger-carrying flights during December 21-31." The problem was later traced to a piece of radio gear separate from the autopilot, the FAA said. Meanwhile, a different MD-83 flew four flights without a fully functioning autopilot after American mechanics put off repairs.  Regulators also accuse American of operating planes without timely inspections of their emergency lighting systems. In April, American canceled more than 3,000 flights to conduct inspections of wiring bundles in wheel wells of its 300 MD-80 jets, snarling air traffic for five days. The FAA ordered American and several other airlines to examine the wiring, which had the potential to start fires or cause landing gear to malfunction.

(CNN) — Federal aviation officials on Thursday proposed $7.1 million in penalties against American Airlines, citing maintenance violations as well as deficiencies in the carrier’s drug- and alcohol-testing procedures.

According to the Federal Aviation Administration, American knowingly continued operating aircraft that required repairs. The agency said the size of the proposed penalty reflects the airline’s decision to postpone necessary maintenance despite being aware of the problems. By deliberately keeping the planes in service, the FAA said, American violated key safety rules designed to protect passengers and crew members.

The airline may appeal the penalties, the FAA noted.

Regulators also determined that American’s drug- and alcohol-testing programs were inadequate and that required inspections of safety lighting were not completed promptly.

American, which is based in Fort Worth, Texas, said Thursday evening that it disputed the FAA’s conclusions and considered the fines excessive. In a written response, the airline said it had asked to meet with agency officials after fully reviewing the findings, in accordance with FAA procedures. Because the matters remain under consideration, American said it would not comment further.

Almost $4.5 million of the proposed penalties involves two MD-83 aircraft that American continued to operate in December 2007 after pilots reported autopilot malfunctions, the FAA said. Together, the two jets completed 58 flights before repairs were made. One of them flew 10 times even after an FAA inspector told the airline that the required work had been improperly postponed.

In one case, an autopilot disengaged during a landing on December 21. The FAA said American’s technicians failed to investigate the underlying cause and instead delayed maintenance by incorrectly applying an item from the minimum equipment list. That aircraft then carried passengers on 36 more flights between December 21 and December 31.

Investigators later determined that the malfunction originated in radio equipment separate from the autopilot system, according to the FAA.

A second MD-83, meanwhile, completed four flights without a fully operational autopilot after American mechanics deferred repairs.

The FAA also alleges that the carrier flew aircraft whose emergency-lighting systems had not been inspected within the required time frame.

In April, American canceled more than 3,000 flights so it could inspect wiring bundles located in the wheel wells of its 300 MD-80 aircraft. The disruption affected air travel for five days. The FAA had directed American and several other carriers to inspect the wiring because it could potentially cause fires or interfere with the operation of landing gear.

**FAA Proposes $7.1 Million in Fines Against American Airlines**

Federal aviation regulators proposed $7.1 million in civil penalties against American Airlines following an investigation that identified several alleged safety and regulatory violations. According to the Federal Aviation Administration, the carrier knowingly postponed required aircraft repairs, failed to properly administer parts of its employee drug- and alcohol-testing program, and did not complete certain safety-lighting inspections on time.

Among the most serious allegations, the FAA said American continued operating two MD-83 aircraft after pilots reported problems with their autopilot systems. The two jets were flown a combined 58 times before the reported issues were properly addressed, regulators said. The agency maintained that allowing the aircraft to remain in service under those circumstances represented a significant breach of federal safety requirements.

The proposed fines also cover alleged deficiencies in American’s management of mandatory drug and alcohol testing for safety-sensitive employees. Federal rules require airlines to maintain testing programs and follow detailed procedures designed to ensure that workers performing critical duties are fit for service.

In addition, the FAA accused American of delaying required inspections of safety-lighting systems. Such inspections are intended to confirm that emergency and other safety-related lighting equipment is functioning correctly and available when needed.

American Airlines disputed the FAA’s conclusions, characterizing the proposed penalties as excessive. The carrier indicated that it wanted further discussions with the agency and would have an opportunity to respond before the fines became final.

The enforcement action underscores the FAA’s position that airlines must promptly resolve reported mechanical problems and comply fully with federal testing, inspection and record-keeping requirements.

**FAA proposes $7.1 million in fines against American Airlines**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Federal Aviation Administration has proposed $7.1 million in civil penalties against American Airlines, alleging the carrier improperly deferred required maintenance and failed to comply with federal drug- and alcohol-testing rules.

The FAA said some aircraft continued operating after maintenance problems were identified but not properly addressed. The agency also cited deficiencies in American’s testing program for employees who perform safety-sensitive work.

The allegations do not represent a final determination. American Airlines will have an opportunity to respond to the FAA and may challenge or negotiate the proposed penalties.

The airline said it takes safety and regulatory compliance seriously and was reviewing the FAA’s claims.

Federal rules allow airlines to postpone certain repairs under approved maintenance procedures, but only when specific conditions and time limits are met. The FAA said American failed to follow those requirements in some cases.

Drug- and alcohol-testing programs are required for pilots, mechanics and other workers whose duties can affect flight safety. Airlines must ensure eligible employees are tested and that records and procedures comply with federal standards.

The proposed fines are among the largest enforcement actions brought by the FAA against a U.S. carrier and come amid heightened scrutiny of airline maintenance practices.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a detailed aviation news article explaining why the FAA fined American Airlines $7.1 million and why the carrier considers the penalties excessive.
counterfactuals.output:
# FAA Seeks $7.1 Million From American Airlines Over Alleged Safety-Compliance Failures

**The penalties center on American’s alleged failure to complete required maintenance and inspections within federally mandated intervals. The airline says the proposed amount is disproportionate because the disputes involve compliance and recordkeeping rather than evidence that its aircraft were unsafe.**

The Federal Aviation Administration has proposed approximately **$7.1 million in civil penalties against American Airlines**, alleging that the carrier operated aircraft that did not fully comply with federal maintenance, inspection and documentation requirements.

Although the action has often been described as a “fine,” it is more precisely a package of **proposed civil penalties**. American can challenge the allegations and the size of the assessments through the FAA’s administrative process before any final amount is imposed.

## Why the FAA proposed the penalties

At the heart of the enforcement action is the FAA’s requirement that airlines follow their approved maintenance programs exactly. Those programs establish when particular inspections, checks and other airworthiness tasks must be performed, how the work must be recorded and who is authorized to return an aircraft to service.

According to the FAA’s case, American failed in some instances to complete or properly document required work by the applicable deadline and then operated affected aircraft on revenue flights. From the regulator’s perspective, an aircraft may be considered noncompliant even if it appears to be functioning normally.

That distinction is important. FAA enforcement does not necessarily require proof that an airplane suffered a mechanical failure or placed passengers in immediate danger. Operating an aircraft after a mandatory inspection or maintenance interval has expired can itself constitute a violation because the airline no longer has the required regulatory basis to show that the aircraft is airworthy.

The proposed total reflects more than one alleged violation and, crucially, the FAA’s ability to count continued operations separately. If an aircraft flies multiple times after a compliance deadline, the agency may treat each flight—or each day of continued noncompliance—as an additional offense. That method can rapidly turn a maintenance or paperwork dispute into a multimillion-dollar case.

## Why recordkeeping matters

Airline maintenance records are not regarded as routine administrative paperwork. They are part of the legal evidence that an aircraft is safe to fly.

Those records must show, among other things:

- What maintenance or inspection was required;
- When it was completed;
- Who performed and approved the work;
- Whether any defects were deferred under an authorized program;
- Whether recurring inspection limits were properly calculated; and
- Whether the aircraft was legally returned to service.

If a task was performed but not documented in the required manner, the FAA may conclude that the airline cannot demonstrate compliance. Similarly, if an airline interprets an inspection interval differently from the FAA, operations conducted under that interpretation may later become the basis for multiple alleged violations.

## Why American calls the amount excessive

American has disputed the size of the proposed penalties, arguing that the FAA’s calculations overstate the seriousness of the events.

The carrier’s position is essentially that the cases involve technical compliance, procedural or recordkeeping questions rather than evidence that it knowingly dispatched unsafe aircraft. American also contends that the agency’s practice of multiplying penalties across individual flights can produce a figure far beyond what is justified by the underlying conduct.

That is a common point of conflict in aviation enforcement. The FAA views every flight conducted without full regulatory compliance as a separate exposure: passengers and crew were carried on each operation, and the airline had a renewed obligation to verify airworthiness before every departure. Airlines, by contrast, often argue that a single underlying mistake should not be converted into hundreds of distinct offenses simply because the aircraft continued to operate before the issue was identified.

American also maintains that the proposed assessments do not adequately account for factors such as:

- The absence of an accident, incident or in-flight malfunction;
- The airline’s corrective action after the issues were discovered;
- Its cooperation with the regulator;
- Whether the required work had actually been performed but was documented incorrectly;
- The technical nature of the disputed requirements; and
- Whether the FAA’s penalty formula is proportionate to the safety risk.

Calling a penalty excessive does not necessarily mean the airline concedes the violations. It can also mean American disputes the FAA’s legal interpretation, the number of violations counted, the proposed amount—or all three.

## A compliance case, not an accident investigation

The enforcement action should not be interpreted as a finding that American’s aircraft were involved in an accident or that passengers were injured. It is primarily a regulatory-compliance case.

Nevertheless, the FAA treats missed maintenance intervals and incomplete airworthiness records seriously because the commercial aviation safety system is built on preventive controls. Regulators do not wait for a component to fail before enforcing inspection requirements. The purpose of mandatory maintenance is to detect wear, damage or deterioration before it becomes operationally significant.

For that reason, the FAA can pursue substantial penalties even when there was no adverse event. In the agency’s view, allowing an airline to escape meaningful consequences simply because nothing failed would weaken the preventive nature of the rules.

## What happens next

American has the right to respond to the FAA’s enforcement notices, submit evidence and request that the allegations or proposed amounts be reduced. The airline and the agency may negotiate a settlement, or American can continue to contest the matter through administrative and legal channels.

Final airline penalties frequently differ from the amounts initially proposed. The outcome can depend on whether American demonstrates that tasks were completed, that records were misunderstood, that fewer flights should be counted or that mitigating factors justify a lower assessment.

The dispute therefore turns on two related but separate questions: **whether American fully complied with the FAA’s maintenance and documentation rules, and whether $7.1 million is a proportionate sanction for the alleged failures**.

For the FAA, the case is about enforcing strict airworthiness controls before a technical lapse leads to a safety event. For American, it is about preventing procedural or documentation disputes from being multiplied into penalties that the carrier believes bear little relationship to the actual risk involved.

**By CNN Staff**  
**Updated [TIME], [DATE]**

**Washington, DC —** The Federal Aviation Administration has proposed multimillion-dollar civil penalties against American Airlines over alleged violations involving aircraft maintenance, safety inspections and employee drug-and-alcohol testing, the agency announced [DAY].

The FAA is seeking a total of **$[AMOUNT] million** in penalties. Regulators allege the carrier operated certain aircraft without completing required maintenance or inspections and failed to comply with federal testing requirements for safety-sensitive employees.

The alleged violations occurred between **[DATE RANGE]**, according to enforcement documents released by the agency.

“The FAA’s safety rules are designed to ensure aircraft are airworthy and employees performing safety-sensitive duties meet federal requirements,” the agency said in a statement.

American Airlines said it is reviewing the allegations and emphasized that the proposed fines are not final.

“Safety is the foundation of everything we do,” the airline said in a statement. “We have cooperated with the FAA throughout its review and will respond through the established administrative process.”

The FAA did not immediately say whether any passengers or crew members were placed in danger as a result of the alleged violations. No injuries have been linked to the cases.

Proposed civil penalties can be challenged, negotiated or reduced before becoming final. American Airlines will have an opportunity to respond to the FAA’s enforcement notices.

The action comes as federal regulators increase scrutiny of airline maintenance practices, quality-control systems and workforce compliance following a series of high-profile aviation safety incidents across the industry.
